name: Silk'n Infinity / Flash&Go

card.summary: Silk'n home light-based hair-removal devices; an early small study of the brand's home pulsed light device reported hair reduction.
card.note: Study data are for an early Silk'n device, not necessarily these models.

quick.overview:
Silk'n makes home light-based hair-removal devices, including the Infinity and Flash&Go lines. They use low-energy pulsed light designed for self-treatment.

A 2009 study of an early Silk'n home pulsed light device tested 34 people and 92 sites with blinded hair counts. Sources on the Infinity and Flash&Go models themselves were not found.
quick.mechanism: Home pulsed light is absorbed by hair melanin, heating the follicle. Silk'n devices are described as small, light, low-energy and low-cost IPL systems.
quick.risks: A 2010 review of home IPL devices noted they are designed to cause biological damage to follicles, with eye safety a key design concern. Home-use IPL is generally considered less suited to very dark skin or light hair.

lead: Silk'n is a brand of home light-based hair-removal devices, including the Infinity and Flash&Go models. An early device from the brand, made by HomeSkinovations of Israel, was described in a 2009 study as a small, light-weight, low-energy, low-cost IPL system for home use. [1]

The 2009 study tested the device on 34 people and 92 sites, with self-treatment supervised in clinic and hair counts done by a blinded observer. [1] The sources reviewed contain no trial specific to the Infinity or Flash&Go models.

paras: A 2009 study of the Silk'n home pulsed light device on 34 people and 92 test sites used pre- and post-treatment hair counts analysed by a blinded observer. [1] A 2014 IRB-approved study of 17 subjects examined the separate Silk'n Blue device for inflammatory acne, with eight treatments over four weeks, and reported a statistically significant decrease in acne lesions. [3] A 2023 study compared a home-use laser with a diode laser for hair reduction. [4]

A 2010 review of home-use IPL devices stated that such systems are designed to cause biological damage and that eye safety is a central design requirement. [2] Encyclopedic sources list hyperpigmentation among IPL complications. [5]

timeline.event: Study of the Silk'n home pulsed light device published. [1]
